newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan budget intended to stimulate economy.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan budget intended to stimulate economy.

text.p: Pakistan's Finance Minister Sartaj Aziz on Friday unveiled a budget for 1997/98 (July-June) designed to stimulate the ailing economy and curb a chronic fiscal deficit.

He allocated 134 billion rupees ($3.3 billion) for defence out of total expenditure of 552 billion rupees, a two percent nominal increase over last year but a decrease in real terms given inflation, now running at about 13 percent.
Pakistan, long at odds with India, is due to host a new round of talks between top foreign ministry officials on Thursday designed to reduce tensions with its giant neighbour.
The total budget outlay of 552 billion rupees represents an increase of 10.4 percent over last year's 500.2 billion.

Aziz told Reuters Financial Television earlier on Friday that apart from debt servicing, he would curb all areas of spending, including defence, to cut the budget deficit to five percent of gross domestic product from this year's 6.2 percent.
"We have continued this policy for the next year to keep a very strong curb on the other expenditure, and that includes defence expenditure," he said.
"We are now focusing on the revival of the economy," he said.
"These are our four critical targets: seven percent industrial growth, five percent agricultural growth, six percent GDP growth, and 15 percent export growth."
This year manufacturing grew an estimated 1.8 percent, agriculture 0.7 percent and gross domestic product 3.1 percent, while exports expanded 1.1 percent in the first nine months.
If Pakistan, mired in what Aziz called a virtual industrial crisis, could meet the targets set out in the budget, "the recovery phase will be over in the next few months".
He voiced confidence that the IMF, which has agreed to start talks in July on a new medium-term loan, would approve of the government's "home-grown" structural reform agenda.
The IMF had been concerned about whether Pakistan would pursue stabilisation measures with equal vigour. "This budget does fully incorporate those concerns," he said.
Aziz said Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif's four-month-old government was determined to carry out structural reforms, rather than simply raising taxes to tackle the fiscal crisis.
A key element in the strategy was to "restructure those institutions that are causing an indirect fiscal haemorrhage" such as state-owned banks, utilities, railways and others.
The finance minister promised to overhaul the tax system because "higher tax rates do not mean higher collection unless the collecting machinery is reformed".
The budget, reinforcing tax cuts unveiled in March, had "withdrawn excessive taxation from many individual industries".
Aziz said inflation could be cut to single figures in 1997/98 if production picked up and money supply was restrained.
